turns.text: What still haunts me is the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I walked straight into a crowd of students—some I had taught, some I barely recognized—who dragged me onto a makeshift stage. They shouted, waved their fists, and accused me of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter. I remember the spit hitting my face, the feeling of my knees buckling as they forced me to kneel. What I can’t make sense of, even now, is how quickly those young people, who once looked to me for guidance, turned into my accusers. It was as if overnight, the trust and respect I had built over decades evaporated, replaced by suspicion and hatred. I still wonder: did they believe what they were saying, or were they afraid not to?

I remember the first time I walked through the gate of my institute after returning from the countryside. The courtyard was plastered with big-character posters—layers upon layers, some so thick you could barely make out the bricks beneath. The air stank of paste and paper, and everywhere I looked, people gathered in tight circles, reading or arguing. No one mentioned research; all talk was about who had the wrong background, who had said the wrong thing. I spent my days reading these posters, sometimes writing one under pressure, never knowing who might be targeted next. 

At home, the situation was worse. My mother, already frail, was sent back to her village in Hebei because her father had been a landlord. She was forced to wear a black sash in public, and I heard from neighbors that children threw stones at her. On the bus, I watched a Red Guard block a young man from giving up his seat to an old woman until she recited her class background. If she had been from a “bad” class, she would have been forced to stand the whole way. I saw women with curled hair yanked into the street so that children could hack off their hair with scissors. I kept my hair in a bun, hoping to avoid that fate.

What I cannot make sense of is how ordinary children—neighbors I’d watched grow up—could suddenly become so cruel. I saw them beating old men with their belts, laughing as they dragged women around by their braids. I still don’t understand how fear and hatred took root so quickly, or why no one—not the Party, not the leaders in my work unit—stood up to stop it.

RedGuard: I can still feel the heat from that bonfire outside the hospital. We had just finished parading the director, the vice directors, and a handful of others through the streets. They wore black placards with their “crimes” scrawled in thick ink, heads bowed, faces streaked with sweat and ash. The crowd jeered, some spat, and a few old nurses wept quietly as we tossed their confiscated books and photos into the flames. I remember the smell—burning paper, scorched wool, something sharp and sour I still can’t name.

Later, when we returned, word spread that one of the nurses had hanged herself. She was young, maybe not much older than I was. I saw her body in the duty room, feet dangling just above the floor, her face already turning grey. Some of us stood there, not speaking. I remember thinking: we had been so sure, so righteous, and now there was this silence, heavier than anything the loudspeakers ever blasted.

What I can’t make sense of is how quickly we acted—how easily I let myself believe every accusation, every rumor. I thought I was fighting for justice, for Mao, for the revolution. But even now, I can still hear her scream from earlier that day, when we shaved her head with that rusted clipper. I don’t know if it was fear, excitement, or something else that kept me moving forward, but I never stopped to question what we were doing—not until it was far too late.

I remember the taste of cold mung bean popsicles, sitting on the stone steps outside our building, the wrapper sticky in my hand. The world inside the compound felt small and safe—soldiers in green uniforms, rows of laundry flapping between trees, the soft thud of a basketball somewhere in the dusk. My little brother and sister chased each other around the benches, and I watched the sky change color, thinking only of what we’d eat for dinner or whether I’d get to paddle the rubber boat on the lake the next day.

Sometimes, we heard shouting from the main road—parades, slogans, drums. Once, I pressed my face to the fence and saw a crowd marching with big red banners, chanting words I didn’t really understand. My mother pulled me back, told me not to stare. At home, I heard adults whispering about someone being sent away, but I didn't know what it meant. School stopped, but I didn’t mind. I played, read comic books, learned to cook rice without burning it. The only fear I remember was when the grown-ups argued in low voices, or when someone’s father didn’t come home for a few days.

Looking back, I can’t make sense of how two worlds existed side by side—one where children like me felt safe and free, another where people were hurt, humiliated, even killed. I didn’t see the pain you talk about, Professor, or the violence you describe, Red Guard. I only saw the bright parts, as if I’d been living behind a thick curtain. Now, I wonder: was that protection, or just blindness?

I remember the day I was handed a form in the barracks. My hands were still dirty from hauling sacks of grain, and the sergeant told me, almost casually, that the unit was recommending me to Beida. I stared at the paper, not even understanding what it meant at first. I thought maybe it was a mistake, or some new kind of mobilization order. No one in my family had ever seen a university, let alone Peking University. I had grown up measuring luck by whether we got half a pumpkin in a distribution, not by grades or exams.

When I arrived in Beijing, I was given a badge and a student ID. The badge was heavy, metal, with bold characters stamped on it. It felt like a piece of armor and a ticket to a new life at the same time. I wore it everywhere, even when I slept, afraid someone would say it wasn’t real. The first time I walked into the canteen, I saw students from the city—clean clothes, leather shoes, easy laughter. I still had straw sandals and the habit of eating quickly, guarding my bowl with my arm.

What I can’t make sense of is how I went from being invisible—just another rural mouth to feed—to being held up as an example, a “worker-peasant-soldier student.” The old rules were gone, but I never understood who decided the new ones. I didn’t know why I was chosen and not the boy next to me in the fields. Some days, I felt like I’d stolen someone else’s life, and I wondered if the ground would open up and drop me back where I started. Even now, I look at that badge and wonder what it really meant: was it a reward, a tool, or just another way the times played with people’s fates?

Moderator: All of your memories reflect the intense uncertainty and rapid reversals of fortune that characterized the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher, your accounts of public humiliation and violence are consistent with the widespread "struggle sessions" and attacks on intellectuals and those with "bad" class backgrounds. RedGuard, your memory of participating in violence and later questioning it reflects the reality that many young people were swept up in the movement, often with tragic consequences. CRTeenFromBeijing, your experience of relative safety in a military compound highlights the unevenness of the era—some urban and military families were insulated from the worst violence, especially in the early years. CRBeneficiary, your story illustrates how new policies upended traditional hierarchies, allowing some from rural or working-class backgrounds to enter elite institutions, though the criteria for selection were often opaque and arbitrary.

Hearing you, Red Guard, describe that bonfire and what followed—how you acted without questioning, how the excitement and fear mixed together—I recognize that energy from the campus, too. I saw it in the eyes of students who’d once been shy, suddenly shouting slogans with their fists in the air. I wonder if you ever felt trapped by that momentum, even as you helped drive it. For me, there was no way to defend myself; if I argued, I was “stubborn,” if I stayed silent, I was “admitting guilt.” 

What I still can’t accept is how Mao Zedong’s words—just a few lines on a poster—could turn ordinary people into enemies overnight. I had argued with his daughter about ideology, about what “class struggle” meant in practice. We disagreed, yes, but I never imagined those arguments would be twisted into evidence of persecution. I wonder, Red Guard, how much you truly believed in what you were doing, and how much you simply feared what would happen if you stopped. Did you ever see doubt in the faces around you, or did everyone seem certain?

When I read your words, Professor, I feel the weight of what was lost—trust, safety, the sense that there were rules we could rely on. In my unit, I saw the same transformation in people’s faces, but from a different angle. The leaders who once guided us, some of them old soldiers from the resistance, suddenly became silent. They didn’t dare speak up, but they also didn’t join in the violence. I watched them shrink into themselves, eyes fixed on the floor during meetings, hands shaking as they signed confessions or apologies they did not believe. 

Outside, the city was wild. I remember one night cycling home—buses were impossible, packed with shouting teenagers—when a jeep screeched to a stop beside me. It was full of workers, laughing and shouting as they swapped out streetlights. They looked so proud, so sure of themselves, as if the world finally belonged to them. Meanwhile, my neighbors and I moved like shadows, careful not to draw attention. 

I still don’t understand how the words of one man could erase all our old bonds so quickly. I didn’t believe in the slogans, but I was afraid to say so—even to my own children. I saw children in our compound imitating the Red Guards, beating each other with belts, practicing struggle sessions on the elderly. I tried to stop them once, and they looked at me as if I were the enemy. 

What did it feel like, Red Guard, to be surrounded by that certainty, to move with the crowd? Did you ever sense the fear in those you targeted? And to the rural student—when you arrived in Beijing, did you feel the city’s chaos, or did your new status protect you from it? I wonder if you ever felt guilty for the way the rules changed in your favor, while others lost everything.

RedGuard: Professor, your question stings because I remember the first time I saw doubt in someone’s eyes—really saw it, up close. It was during a house search, an old teacher’s apartment, the walls lined with foreign books and photographs. She looked at me—not with hatred, not even fear, but confusion, as if she couldn’t believe I was the same boy who used to run errands for her. In that moment, my hands shook, but the others kept shouting, so I shouted too. The momentum you mention—it was like being swept by a flood. If you hesitated, even for a second, someone else would push you aside, or worse, turn on you. I wanted to believe I was on the right side, because the alternative—admitting you were wrong, or even just unsure—was unthinkable. The crowd was always watching.

Researcher, I absolutely sensed the fear. Sometimes it made me feel powerful, other times it made me sick. The first time I poured ink over a teacher’s head, my heart raced—not from joy, but from the terror that if I didn’t do it, I’d be next. I saw people break down, cry, beg. I told myself they deserved it, that Mao’s words were truth. But at night, lying on a straw mat, I’d replay faces in my mind and wonder if I’d crossed a line that could never be uncrossed.

As for guilt, it came in waves—especially after my own family was labeled “black.” Suddenly, I was on the other side of the slogans. I saw how fast labels changed, how arbitrary it all was. I still can’t decide if I was a true believer or just afraid to be left behind. And I wonder, CRBeneficiary, when you wore that badge, did you ever look at someone who had lost everything and wonder if it was worth it? Did you ever feel that your new status was built on someone else’s ruin?

I never felt the weight of those labels the way you all describe. In our compound, everyone wore the same kind of blue cotton jacket, ate the same food, and followed the same routines. I didn’t know who was “red” or “black”—those words floated around, but they didn’t stick to anyone I could see. The only time I sensed something was wrong was when a neighbor’s apartment was suddenly empty. My mother told me not to ask questions, so I didn’t. I just noticed the silence where there used to be laughter and the smell of fried eggs.

Sometimes, I’d see posters pasted on the walls outside the compound—big characters, red ink, names crossed out. I couldn’t read most of the words, but I liked the way the paper crinkled in the wind. Once, I watched a group of Red Guards march past our gate, armbands bright, faces serious. They looked older than me, but not by much. I felt a strange mix of envy and fear—envy because they seemed so important, fear because I didn’t understand what they were fighting for.

Now, hearing all of you, I wonder if my ignorance was a kind of luck. I was never told to shout slogans or write posters. I never had to choose between joining in or being silent. But I also never questioned anything. I just accepted that the world was divided and that I was on the safe side of the fence. Did you ever wish you could go back to that kind of innocence, or did you feel that knowing—even if it hurt—was better than not seeing at all?

When I first arrived in Beijing, the chaos of the city was unavoidable. I remember stepping off the army truck and seeing walls covered in red slogans, crowds pressing around university gates, and students shouting at each other in accents I barely understood. The canteen line was tense—people glancing at my badge, some with curiosity, others with a kind of calculation. I could feel the city’s energy, but I didn’t know the rules. I kept my head down, copied what the others did, and tried not to draw attention.

My new status protected me from some things, but not from feeling out of place. I was always aware that my “good” background was why I’d been picked. I saw others—older professors, city students from the “wrong” class—move quietly, eyes lowered, always polite but never relaxed. One night, I watched a group of students paste up a new list of names on the dormitory wall. I recognized a few from the canteen. The next morning, those students were gone. No explanation, just empty beds and whispers. I realized then that my own place was never secure; it depended on staying in favor, on fitting the image the authorities wanted.

Red Guard, you ask if I ever wondered if my status was built on someone else’s ruin. I did. I saw the professors who taught us—some looked proud, others broken. I didn’t know what they’d done or what they’d lost. I knew only that I was there because someone else couldn’t be. I felt lucky, but also uneasy, as if my fortune was borrowed and could be taken back at any moment. I didn’t believe in the slogans, but I learned to repeat them. I wanted to survive, to hold onto what I’d been given, even if it was at the expense of someone else’s life being turned upside down.

As for innocence, I never had it. Hunger teaches you early that the world isn’t fair. Seeing how quickly the rules could change in Beijing only made me more determined to take what I could before it vanished. I never felt guilt the way you describe, Red Guard, but I did feel fear—fear that the ground would shift again and I’d be back in the fields, or worse. I wonder, for those who lost everything, did they ever think the system would turn back in their favor, or did they just learn to keep their heads down and wait?

Moderator: The discussion reflects the unstable social hierarchy and pervasive fear that shaped daily life during the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher, your experiences of arbitrary accusation and the collapse of authority are accurate—many leaders and intellectuals were powerless to protect themselves or others. RedGuard, your account of shifting from perpetrator to victim mirrors the reality that political labels could change overnight, and former Red Guards themselves were later targeted. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sheltered perspective is plausible; military compounds often provided a buffer from violence, especially for children, though not always indefinitely. CRBeneficiary, your sense of precarious privilege highlights that “worker-peasant-soldier” admissions were both an opportunity and a source of anxiety, as social mobility during the Cultural Revolution was unpredictable and often came at the expense of others.
